newsitem.title: UK: Churches mark 1,400 years of English Christianity.
newsitem.headline: Churches mark 1,400 years of English Christianity.

text.p: Leaders of the Anglican and Catholic Churches joined forces on Sunday to mark the 1,400th anniversary of St Augustine's landing in England, an event usually seen as marking Christianity's arrival in the country.

Archbishop of Canterbury George Carey, the senior clergyman in the Church of England, and Catholic Cardinal Basil Hume officiated at a service on the north Kent coast at the spot where Augustine is traditionally supposed to have landed in 597.
They were joined by 300 pilgrims who for the past week have been following the route the founder of English Christianity took from Rome, a spokeswoman for Carey said.

After the Romans left England in the fifth century, pagan invaders flooded in from Scandinavia and what is now northern Germany, forcing Christianity to retreat to Wales, Ireland and the Celtic area of Cornwall in the extreme south-west.

Pope Gregory chose Augustine to lead a band of some 40 monks on a missionary journey to Kent, south-east England where he was welcomed by King Ethelbert and given a house at Canterbury, where Carey's cathedral is now sited.
During the 90 years after Augustine's landing, all the Saxon kingdoms of England accepted the faith.
"In terms of English history the coming of Augustine represents a watershed," Carey said.
"Essentially, tools like literacy and learning had effectively disappeared. Augustine bought with him learning."
